abstract: Efficient photosynthesis is crucial to agricultural productivity and can be constrained by the plant carbon-nitrogen balance, offering an opportunity for genetic improvement. Furthermore, soil N availability limits grain yields, and crops require substantial N fertilizer to be productive. In C4 plants, carbon-concentrating mechanisms respond to decreased soil nitrogen and share molecular intermediates with N metabolism. Maize, one of the most widely grown crops globally, uses a combination of two C4 photosynthetic pathways. Most carbon fixation occurs through the NADP-malic enzyme (NADP-ME) pathway, yet some fixation is also thought to occur via phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK). However, genetic evidence for the contribution of PEPCK is lacking. Here, we used a transposon-based mutagenesis approach to study the function of the C4 isoform of PEPCK1 in maize. The C4 pathway intermediate aspartate accumulated to high concentrations in the leaves of the pepck1-2::Ds knock-down mutant, providing genetic support for the PEPCK secondary pathway as a complement to the dominant NADP-ME shuttle in maize. Field experiments over multiple seasons in either N-limiting or N-sufficient soils demonstrated the pepck1::Ds mutants produced higher vegetative and grain biomass without changes in leaf photosynthetic rates or parameters. This study confirms that PEPCK1 catalyzes the decarboxylation of carbon shuttled as aspartate, as an alternative route to decarboxylation by NADP-ME in a nominally NADP-ME subtype C4 species maize, providing clear genetic support for two-pathway operation. Further, the greater resilience and N-responsiveness of mutant plants are valuable traits for sustainable and subsistence farming in the future.
